title: Diseases of the Upper Respiratory Tract
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers infection and inflammation of the conducting airway from the nose to the large bronchi: acute bronchitis, epiglottitis, laryngitis, croup, bacterial tracheitis, rhinitis, sinusitis, pharyngitis, and tonsillitis. Most of these conditions are common and self-limited, so board questions focus on telling them apart and on predicting the few dangerous outcomes. The anatomy does most of the work: where the swelling sits explains the voice, the cough, the stridor, and the radiograph, and the venous and bony relations of the sinuses and tonsils explain how infection spreads. The microbiology and immunology explain the rest, from why rhinovirus stays in the nose to why a sore throat can damage a heart valve weeks later.

connections.to: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system (PU-14-H)
connections.how: Pertussis, pneumonia, and influenza continue the same infections into the lower airway, where alveolar filling adds consolidation.
Chronic bronchitis is defined by a persistent productive cough from sustained mucus hypersecretion, often with airflow obstruction, which acute bronchitis lacks.
Allergic rhinitis is a type I reaction, rheumatic fever a type II reaction, and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis a type III reaction.
Repeated rheumatic carditis after streptococcal pharyngitis is the classic cause of mitral stenosis.
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is the prototype nephritic syndrome caused by immune complex deposition.

sections.title: Acute bronchitis and how it differs from pneumonia and chronic bronchitis

blocks.text: Acute bronchitis is inflammation of the trachea and large bronchi that produces cough, with or without sputum, lasting up to about 3 weeks. About 90% or more of cases are viral: influenza, parainfluenza, respiratory syncytial virus, coronaviruses, adenovirus, and rhinovirus. A small minority are bacterial, mainly Bordetella pertussis, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia pneumoniae (pertussis is taught in PU-14-H). Smoking and air pollution increase the risk and prolong the cough.

The viruses infect the ciliated columnar cells of the pseudostratified epithelium. Infected cells lose their cilia and slough, so mucociliary clearance fails while goblet cells and submucosal glands increase secretion. The denuded, inflamed mucosa exposes and sensitizes vagal irritant receptors and C fibers, so minor stimuli trigger cough. Regrowth of the epithelium from basal cells takes weeks, which is why the cough outlasts the fever and why transient airway hyperresponsiveness with mild wheeze is common. Sputum may turn yellow or green; the color comes from neutrophil myeloperoxidase, a green heme enzyme, and does not by itself mean bacterial infection.

The key distinction from pneumonia is location. Acute bronchitis stays in the conducting airways, so the alveoli remain filled with air. There is no consolidation on chest radiograph, no focal dullness, bronchial breath sounds, or egophony, and gas exchange is preserved. Pneumonia fills alveoli with exudate, which adds high fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, focal crackles, a new infiltrate, and often hypoxemia from right-to-left shunting through the filled units.

Chronic bronchitis is a separate disease, not a long episode of acute bronchitis. It is defined clinically as a productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, results from sustained irritant exposure (mostly tobacco smoke), and shows submucosal gland hyperplasia (Reid index above 0.5), goblet cell metaplasia, and, when small airways are involved, progressive airflow obstruction (PU-14-B). A viral bronchitis in someone with COPD is an acute exacerbation of that chronic disease.

sections.title: Epiglottitis and the risk of sudden airway obstruction

blocks.text: Epiglottitis (supraglottitis) is a bacterial cellulitis of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, and arytenoid regions. The epiglottis is elastic cartilage covered by mucosa, and on its lingual surface and the aryepiglottic folds the submucosa is loose areolar tissue, so inflammatory edema accumulates quickly and the structure can swell to several times its normal size within hours.

The classic cause is Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) in an unvaccinated child about 2 to 7 years old. Hib is a gram-negative coccobacillus that needs factors X (hemin) and V (NAD) to grow. Its polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP) capsule resists phagocytosis and complement-mediated killing, allowing bacteremia and invasive disease. Young children respond poorly to polysaccharide antigens, which are T cell independent, so they are especially vulnerable. Conjugate vaccines link PRP to a protein carrier, recruiting helper T cells and producing protective antibody in infancy, which is why epiglottitis is now rare in vaccinated children. Current cases occur more often in adults and may involve Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, or nontypeable H. influenzae.

Each classic sign follows from supraglottic swelling. Swallowing over an inflamed epiglottis is very painful, so saliva pools and the child drools and refuses to swallow (dysphagia, odynophagia). The voice is muffled rather than hoarse, because the vocal folds themselves are spared. The child sits upright, leaning forward on the hands with the neck extended and chin forward (tripod posture), which pulls the tongue and epiglottis forward and opens the laryngeal inlet. Onset is sudden with high fever, often 39 to 40 °C (102.2 to 104 °F), and a toxic appearance; the barking cough of croup is usually absent. A lateral neck radiograph shows the thumb sign, a rounded, enlarged epiglottis.

blocks.title: Epiglottitis to airway obstruction
steps: Hib colonizing the nasopharynx invades supraglottic tissue
Cellulitis of loose supraglottic submucosa

Drooling, muffled voice, tripod posture

Sudden complete obstruction and respiratory arrest
blocks.caption: Obstruction can happen within hours of onset; stridor is a late sign that the inlet is already critically narrowed.

blocks.text: The enlarged epiglottis is held clear of the laryngeal inlet mainly by posture. Lying supine lets it fall back over the glottis, and crying or pharyngeal stimulation can provoke laryngospasm, so a child who looked stable can obstruct abruptly.

blocks.predict: Why does a child with epiglottitis have a muffled voice without a barking cough, while a child with croup is hoarse and barks?
blocks.explain: Epiglottitis swells tissue above the vocal folds and spares them, so voice is muffled by the mass in the pharynx; croup inflames the vocal folds and subglottis, so they vibrate abnormally and the narrowed subglottis produces the bark.

sections.title: Acute laryngitis, croup, and bacterial tracheitis

blocks.text: Acute laryngitis is inflammation of the laryngeal mucosa, usually from respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, parainfluenza, influenza, adenovirus) or vocal strain, less often from irritants or acid reflux. Edema in the superficial lamina propria of the vocal folds (Reinke space) adds mass and stiffness, so the folds vibrate irregularly and the voice becomes hoarse or is lost. In the wide adult larynx this swelling seldom narrows the airway enough to cause stridor, and the patient is not toxic.

Croup is viral laryngotracheobronchitis of children about 6 months to 3 years old, mostly in autumn and winter. Parainfluenza virus, an enveloped negative-sense RNA paramyxovirus with hemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion proteins, causes most cases, type 1 most often; respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, and adenovirus cause the rest. After 1 to 2 days of coryza, the child develops a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor, usually worse at night and with agitation, with low-grade fever and a nontoxic appearance.

The subglottis is surrounded by the cricoid, the only complete cartilage ring in the airway, so edema there cannot expand outward and narrows the lumen inward. Because resistance to laminar flow rises with the fourth power of a falling radius (Poiseuille law), a millimeter of edema matters far more in a small child. The stridor is inspiratory because this segment is extrathoracic: during inspiration, pressure inside the airway falls below atmospheric pressure and the narrowed segment collapses further. A frontal neck radiograph shows the steeple sign, a tapered subglottic narrowing.

blocks.caption: The cricoid ring and the child's small airway radius explain why croup obstructs and why the obstruction is heard on inspiration.

blocks.text: Bacterial tracheitis is a secondary bacterial infection of the subglottic trachea, usually after viral injury to the epithelium (often influenza or parainfluenza). Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA, is the most common cause; Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and nontypeable H. influenzae also occur. It begins like croup but the child becomes toxic with high fever, and thick purulent secretions and sloughed pseudomembranes fill the trachea and can obstruct it. A lateral film may show irregular, ragged tracheal margins.

blocks.title: Causes of hoarseness and stridor in children
rows: Hib (unvaccinated); now also streptococci, S. aureus
S. aureus after a viral infection
blocks.caption: Acute laryngitis differs from all three: hoarseness alone in a nontoxic patient, without stridor.

blocks.title: Why 1 mm of edema obstructs a child
blocks.text: Take an infant subglottis about 4 mm across (radius 2 mm) and, for comparison, an airway twice as wide, 8 mm across (radius 4 mm); a real adult subglottis is wider still. Add 1 mm of circumferential edema. The infant radius falls from 2 to 1 mm: cross-sectional area falls by 75%, and laminar resistance, proportional to 1 divided by radius to the fourth power, rises 2 to the fourth, or 16-fold. The wider radius falls from 4 to 3 mm: area falls by about 44%, and resistance rises (4/3) to the fourth, about 3-fold. Flow through the narrowed segment also becomes turbulent, heard as stridor, which raises resistance further. The same viral swelling that makes an adult hoarse can make a toddler struggle to breathe.

The nasal mucosa warms, humidifies, and filters inspired air. The turbinates contain venous sinusoids (erectile capacitance vessels) whose filling sets nasal patency. Sympathetic alpha-adrenergic tone constricts them and opens the airway, while parasympathetic fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion drive glandular secretion and vasodilation. Rhinitis is inflammation or dysfunction of this mucosa causing congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, or itch, and the three main forms differ in what drives it.

Allergic rhinitis is a type I hypersensitivity. At sensitization, dendritic cells present allergen to naive T cells, Th2 cells release IL-4 and IL-13, and B cells switch to IgE, which binds the high-affinity Fc epsilon receptor I on mast cells. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links bound IgE. The early phase follows within minutes: histamine stimulates sensory nerves (itch and sneezing) and makes venules leak (clear rhinorrhea and swollen turbinates), and leukotrienes and prostaglandin D2 add congestion. The late phase follows hours later as IL-5 recruits eosinophils and Th2 cells sustain the inflammation, causing persistent congestion. Turbinates look pale, boggy, and bluish from submucosal edema; nasal smears show eosinophils and serum IgE may be raised. Allergic shiners (dark infraorbital venous congestion) and a transverse nasal crease from repeated upward rubbing are common in children. Disease is seasonal with pollens or perennial with dust mites, animal dander, cockroach, and molds, and often accompanies asthma and atopic dermatitis.

blocks.text: Infectious rhinitis is mostly the common cold, and rhinovirus causes the largest share (roughly 30 to 50%). Rhinovirus is a small, nonenveloped, positive-sense RNA picornavirus. It is acid labile, so it does not survive the stomach and is not an enteric pathogen, unlike the related acid-stable enteroviruses. It replicates best at about 33 to 35 °C (91.4 to 95 °F), the temperature of the nasal passages. The major group of serotypes binds ICAM-1 (CD54) on nasal epithelium, and well over 100 serotypes explain repeated colds. The virus causes little cell death; symptoms come from host mediators such as bradykinin and IL-8, so the mucosa is red and swollen with neutrophils, and watery discharge turns mucopurulent.

Vasomotor rhinitis is nonallergic and noninfectious. Temperature change, strong odors, alcohol, or spicy food trigger congestion and watery rhinorrhea, thought to reflect autonomic imbalance with relative parasympathetic dominance and hyperreactive sensory nerves. IgE, skin tests, and nasal eosinophils are normal.

blocks.title: Three forms of rhinitis
blocks.caption: Eosinophils and pale mucosa point to allergy; neutrophils and red mucosa point to infection.

sections.title: Sinusitis: ostial obstruction, organisms, and complications

blocks.text: The paranasal sinuses are air spaces lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium, and they stay healthy only while cilia sweep mucus out through narrow ostia. The maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain through the ostiomeatal complex in the middle meatus, the posterior ethmoid cells into the superior meatus, and the sphenoid into the sphenoethmoidal recess. The maxillary ostium lies high on the medial wall, so drainage depends on cilia rather than gravity. Only the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are well formed at birth, so ethmoid disease is prominent in young children.

Sinusitis begins when mucosal swelling closes an ostium. Most episodes follow a viral cold; allergic rhinitis, polyps, and septal deviation also obstruct drainage. Behind the blocked ostium, secretions accumulate with low oxygen tension and pH, which impairs ciliary beating and neutrophil killing. Most acute rhinosinusitis stays viral; only a small fraction of colds (often quoted as about 0.5 to 2%) become bacterial, when organisms that colonize the nasopharynx overgrow in the trapped fluid: Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Bacterial infection is suggested by symptoms lasting more than about 10 days without improvement, a severe onset with high fever and purulent discharge, or worsening after initial improvement. Maxillary molar roots lie just below the sinus floor, so dental infection causes sinusitis with oral anaerobes, and poor clearance in cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia causes chronic sinusitis (more than 12 weeks).

Complications follow the anatomy. The lamina papyracea, a paper-thin plate of ethmoid bone, separates the ethmoid cells from the orbit, so ethmoid infection reaches the orbit and causes orbital cellulitis: proptosis, painful and limited eye movement; preseptal cellulitis, in front of the orbital septum, swells the eyelid but spares eye movement. The ophthalmic veins, classically described as valveless, connect the face, orbit, and sinuses to the cavernous sinus, so ethmoid or sphenoid infection can cause septic cavernous sinus thrombosis. Cranial nerves III, IV, V1, and V2 run in its lateral wall and CN VI runs within it beside the internal carotid artery, producing ophthalmoplegia (often lateral gaze first), ptosis, forehead and cheek numbness, and chemosis, often becoming bilateral. Frontal sinusitis can cause frontal bone osteomyelitis, epidural or subdural abscess, meningitis, and brain abscess.

blocks.text: Mucormycosis is the classic sinus infection of diabetic ketoacidosis. Rhizopus and Mucor species form broad, ribbon-like hyphae with few or no septa that branch at wide angles, near 90 degrees. Acidosis releases iron from transferrin, which these fungi need for growth, while hyperglycemia and acidosis impair neutrophil chemotaxis and killing; neutropenia, high-dose glucocorticoids, and deferoxamine (used by the fungus as a siderophore) are other risks. The hyphae invade arteries, causing thrombosis and infarction, so black necrotic eschar appears on the turbinates or palate. Infection spreads into the orbit and brain (rhinocerebral mucormycosis) and can thrombose the cavernous sinus and internal carotid artery.

blocks.predict: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis develops facial swelling, a black lesion on the palate, and loss of eye movement on one side. What organism and what mechanism explain each finding?
blocks.explain: Mucorales (Rhizopus or Mucor) thrive on iron freed by acidosis and evade impaired neutrophils; angioinvasion infarcts the palate (black eschar) and spreads through the orbit to the cavernous sinus, paralyzing CN III, IV, and VI.

sections.title: Streptococcal and viral pharyngitis and the poststreptococcal sequelae

blocks.text: Most pharyngitis is viral. Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococcus) causes roughly 15 to 30% of cases in children, peaking at ages 5 to 15, and fewer in adults. It is a gram-positive coccus in chains, catalase negative and beta-hemolytic, producing complete lysis through streptolysin O (oxygen labile and immunogenic) and streptolysin S (oxygen stable). It is bacitracin sensitive and PYR positive, and its Lancefield group A cell wall carbohydrate is the antigen detected by rapid tests. M protein is the main virulence factor: it binds the complement regulator factor H and fibrinogen, which limits C3b deposition and phagocytosis. A hyaluronic acid capsule that resembles host tissue adds resistance, and pyrogenic exotoxins act as superantigens in scarlet fever.

The findings reflect where the organism grows. Group A streptococcus infects the tonsils and pharynx but not the larynx or bronchi, so the illness is a sudden sore throat with fever, tonsillar exudate rich in neutrophils, palatal petechiae, and tender anterior cervical nodes (the jugulodigastric node drains the tonsil), without cough, coryza, hoarseness, or conjunctivitis. Respiratory viruses infect epithelium throughout the airway, which is why cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, and conjunctivitis point to a viral cause. Specific viral clues include conjunctivitis with adenovirus (pharyngoconjunctival fever) and posterior pharyngeal vesicles with coxsackie A virus (herpangina). In scarlet fever, the exotoxins add a fine sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor, and later desquamation.

blocks.title: Streptococcal versus viral pharyngitis
rows: Rapid antigen test or culture positive
blocks.caption: Fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, and no cough together favor group A streptococcus; no single feature is diagnostic.

blocks.text: Suppurative complications spread locally: peritonsillar and retropharyngeal abscess, otitis media, and sinusitis. The nonsuppurative sequelae are immune mediated and appear after a latent period. Acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis, not skin infection, about 2 to 4 weeks later. Antibodies and T cells directed at M protein and the group A carbohydrate cross-react with cardiac myosin, valve proteins, and other host molecules (molecular mimicry, a type II reaction), producing carditis with Aschoff bodies, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules. Repeated attacks scar the valves, the mitral valve most often. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows pharyngeal or skin infection with nephritogenic strains; immune complexes deposit in glomeruli and activate complement (type III), lowering serum C3 and causing a nephritic syndrome.

blocks.title: The two nonsuppurative sequelae
rows: About 1 to 3 weeks after throat; 3 to 6 weeks after skin
Raised antistreptolysin O or anti-DNase B
Low C3, raised anti-DNase B or ASO
Hematuria, edema, hypertension; most children recover
blocks.caption: Rheumatic fever needs a throat infection; glomerulonephritis can follow throat or skin.

blocks.predict: Why can impetigo cause glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever?
blocks.explain: Glomerulonephritis depends on immune complexes from nephritogenic strains, which can infect skin or throat; rheumatic fever follows only pharyngeal infection, for reasons not fully established.

sections.title: Tonsillitis, infectious mononucleosis, and peritonsillar abscess

blocks.text: The palatine tonsils lie in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches and form part of the ring of pharyngeal lymphoid tissue (Waldeyer ring). Deep crypts lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium sample antigens for underlying lymphoid follicles. A fibrous capsule separates each tonsil from the superior constrictor muscle, and the loose tissue between them is the peritonsillar space. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies both the tonsil and the middle ear, so tonsillar pain is referred to the ear. Exudative tonsillitis is caused by group A streptococcus (C06) or viruses, most importantly Epstein-Barr virus.

Infectious mononucleosis is primary Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, human herpesvirus 4) infection in adolescents and young adults, spread in saliva. EBV, an enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus, infects oropharyngeal epithelium and then B cells, binding CD21 (complement receptor 2) through glycoprotein gp350 and using HLA class II as a coreceptor. Infected B cells proliferate, and a large cytotoxic CD8 T cell response controls them. Those reactive T cells are the atypical lymphocytes (large cells whose abundant cytoplasm indents around red cells), often more than 10% of lymphocytes. Their expansion in lymph nodes, spleen, and liver produces generalized lymphadenopathy, most notably posterior cervical, splenomegaly in about half of patients, and mild hepatitis with raised transaminases. The stretched splenic capsule can rupture, usually within the first few weeks.

Polyclonal B cell activation produces heterophile IgM antibodies that agglutinate sheep or horse red cells (Monospot test). This test can be negative early in the illness and in young children, when EBV-specific antibodies (IgM to viral capsid antigen) confirm acute infection.

Peritonsillar abscess, the most common deep neck infection of adolescents and young adults, forms when tonsillitis spreads through the capsule into the peritonsillar space, usually on one side, and the pus is often polymicrobial: S. pyogenes, S. aureus, and oral anaerobes such as Fusobacterium and Prevotella. The mass pushes the tonsil medially and the soft palate downward and forward, so the uvula deviates to the opposite side. Inflammation spreads to the adjacent medial pterygoid, causing trismus, and the bulging immobile palate gives a muffled hot potato voice with drooling and severe one-sided odynophagia. Spread into the parapharyngeal space threatens the airway and the internal jugular vein (septic thrombophlebitis).

rows: EBV infecting B cells via CD21
Uvula deviated away, trismus, hot potato voice
blocks.caption: Both strep and EBV cause exudate; posterior nodes, splenomegaly, and atypical lymphocytes point to EBV, while unilateral bulging and trismus point to abscess.

blocks.title: Working through an exudative sore throat
blocks.text: A 17-year-old has 6 days of sore throat, fever, and exhaustion. The tonsils are covered in exudate, posterior cervical nodes are enlarged, and the spleen tip is palpable. Exudate alone does not separate strep from EBV. The posterior nodes and splenomegaly point to EBV, because the virus drives B cell proliferation and a CD8 T cell response throughout lymphoid tissue, whereas group A streptococcus inflames only the tonsil and its draining anterior nodes. The blood film would show atypical lymphocytes, and a heterophile test would likely be positive. Later one-sided pain, trismus, and a uvula pushed to the left would instead indicate a right peritonsillar abscess.

integration.text: Anatomy predicts most of this chapter. Where swelling sits relative to the vocal folds decides the voice (muffled above, hoarse at the folds) and the radiograph (thumb above, steeple below), and the extrathoracic position of the larynx and trachea explains why their obstruction is heard on inspiration. The thin lamina papyracea and the venous connections to the cavernous sinus explain orbital and intracranial spread from the sinuses, and the peritonsillar space and its neighbor, the medial pterygoid, explain trismus.

Microbiology and immunology explain the rest. Rhinovirus temperature preference and acid lability keep it in the nose; the Hib capsule and the response of young children to polysaccharide explain the old age pattern of epiglottitis and its decline after conjugate vaccination; and the three hypersensitivity types appear side by side, with IgE in allergic rhinitis, mimicry in rheumatic fever, and immune complexes in glomerulonephritis. The classic presentations are teaching models: vaccinated children now rarely have Hib, adult epiglottitis is more common than pediatric, and exam findings overlap, so the full pattern, not one sign, separates the conditions.

summary: Acute bronchitis is a mostly viral inflammation of the trachea and large bronchi with cough up to about 3 weeks; no consolidation separates it from pneumonia, and the time course and chronic irritant exposure separate it from chronic bronchitis.
Epiglottitis is supraglottic cellulitis, classically Hib in unvaccinated children, with sudden fever, drooling, muffled voice, tripod posture, a thumb sign, and risk of sudden complete obstruction.
Croup is parainfluenza laryngotracheobronchitis of children 6 months to 3 years; edema inside the cricoid ring causes barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and the steeple sign.
Bacterial tracheitis, usually S. aureus after a viral infection, looks like croup in a toxic child with purulent tracheal secretions; acute laryngitis causes hoarseness without stridor.

Allergic rhinitis is type I hypersensitivity with pale boggy mucosa and eosinophils; rhinovirus, an acid-labile picornavirus binding ICAM-1 and preferring nasal temperature, is the main cause of colds; vasomotor rhinitis lacks IgE and eosinophils.
Sinusitis starts with ostial obstruction, is mostly viral, and when bacterial is caused by S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis.

Ethmoid sinusitis reaches the orbit through the lamina papyracea and the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins, affecting CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI; mucormycosis in ketoacidosis causes black necrotic eschar by angioinvasion.

Group A streptococcal pharyngitis causes fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, and no cough; M protein is the main virulence factor and the target of molecular mimicry in rheumatic fever after pharyngitis only.
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows throat or skin infection through immune complex deposition with low C3.

Infectious mononucleosis (EBV via CD21 on B cells) causes exudative tonsillitis with posterior nodes, splenomegaly, atypical CD8 T cells, and heterophile antibodies; peritonsillar abscess causes uvular deviation away from the abscess, trismus, and a muffled voice.

verify: The share of acute bronchitis that is viral is quoted from about 90% to above 95% in different sources; the chapter uses about 90% or more.

The narrowest point of the pediatric airway is taught as the cricoid ring, but imaging studies suggest the glottis and immediate subglottis are functionally narrowest; confirm the wording NABNE expects.
The airway diameters in the croup worked example (about 4 mm infant subglottis, 8 mm comparison airway) are rounded teaching values, and Poiseuille law strictly applies to laminar flow.
Parainfluenza type 1 is given as the most common cause of croup in most sources, with type 3 or 2 in some; confirm if a specific type is tested.
The usual age of bacterial tracheitis and the share caused by S. aureus vary by source.

Rhinovirus share of common colds (about 30 to 50%), optimal temperature (about 33 to 35 °C (91.4 to 95 °F)), and serotype count vary between texts; ICAM-1 binding applies to the major receptor group, while the minor group uses LDL receptor family members and rhinovirus C uses CDHR3.
Criteria for suspecting bacterial sinusitis (more than 10 days, severe onset, double worsening) and the 0.5 to 2% figure come from clinical guidelines; confirm the version NABNE uses.
Facial and ophthalmic veins are classically taught as valveless; anatomic studies show valves in some individuals, so the chapter uses the classic description with that qualifier.

The proportion of pharyngitis due to group A streptococcus (about 15 to 30% in children, fewer in adults) and the latent periods of rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis are approximate and vary by source.
The heterophile test false-negative rate early in illness and in children, and the period of highest splenic rupture risk, vary between sources and are stated without fixed values.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: neck-radiograph-signs (lateral thumb sign versus frontal steeple sign), sinus-drainage (ostiomeatal complex and sinus ostia), and cavernous-sinus (cranial nerves and internal carotid artery in coronal section).
